Preprocessing - From the PsychAD atlas to an analysable HBCC cohort

Donor selection, data reading, quality control, standard single-cell pipeline and pseudobulk matrix

Author

Myriam Sijlimassi

NoteHow to read this notebook

Each step starts with a short explanation of what we do and why, then the code. Every figure comes with:

  • a legend (“Figure PP-Fxx”), written so that it can be copied into the report or the appendix;
  • a “How to read” box, to understand the figure without knowing the method;
  • an “Interpretation” box with the HBCC results.

The whole analysis runs in this notebook. The technical functions (reading the .h5ad file block by block, building the pseudobulk matrix, the selection criteria) are in scripts/utils_h5ad.R and scripts/utils_donors.R.

First render: about 30 minutes plus the download (the .h5ad file of the HBCC cohort weighs about 14 GB and is downloaded once into 01_DATA/raw/). The three heavy steps (nucleus metadata, Seurat object, pseudobulk matrix) save their result in 01_DATA/processed/; the next renders reload these files and take about one minute. To recompute a step, delete its file.

Figures are saved as .png (300 dpi) in 04_FIGURES/preprocessing/. References are numbered in square brackets and listed at the end.

1 Overview

1.1 Question and role of the preprocessing

Central question of the project. Do schizophrenia (SCZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) share cell-type-specific molecular alterations in the human prefrontal cortex, and could these changes reflect accelerated ageing and affect neuronal and glial signalling networks?

Role of this notebook. The PsychAD atlas [1] contains 6.3 million nuclei from 1,494 donors and several brain banks. We extract from it a cohort that can answer the question without obvious bias, and we prepare the data sets used by Q1 to Q5:

Output Content Used by
Donor selection 224 donors, Table 1, inclusion and exclusion criteria, E7 table every question
Nuclei per donor and subclass number of nuclei of each subclass in each donor (all nuclei) Q1 (composition)
Seurat object about 45,000 nuclei (at most 200 per donor), normalised, PCA, UMAP visualisation, Q4 (CellChat)
Pseudobulk matrix 34,176 genes x 6,048 columns (donor x subclass), raw counts Q2 (differential expression), Q5

1.2 The principle behind every step

We compare people, not cells. A brain that gives 5,000 nuclei is still one person. Treating nuclei as independent samples (pseudoreplication) makes p-values far too small [2]. Every test of the project is therefore done at the donor level, and the preprocessing is built for that.

1.3 Plan

The notebook has two parts: first we decide who we compare (study design), then we prepare the data of these donors (data processing).

Part Step What we do Output
A - Study design 1 The data: download the HBCC file, read the table of the nuclei 1,486,324 nuclei, 300 donors
2 Donor selection (inclusion and exclusion criteria) flow table, PP-F01
3 Description of the groups (Table 1) and check of the clinical information tables, PP-F02
4 Sensitivity analyses: group sizes when one criterion changes table
5 Cell types per donor (input of Q1) E7 table
B - Data processing 6 Reading the data, one donor at a time Seurat object
7 Quality control PP-F03
8 Normalisation and visual check of the cell types (PCA, UMAP, marker genes) PP-F04 to PP-F07
9 Pseudobulk (input of Q2 and Q5) pseudobulk matrix

All our choices are gathered in one place. They were fixed before looking at any result.

Parameter Value Why
age_min 20 years end of the developmental transcriptomic remodelling of the cortex [3]
keep_tardive_dyskinesia yes part of the real clinical picture of SCZ (side effect of antipsychotics)
keep_metabolic_controls yes controls with diabetes or atherosclerosis are tolerated in [1]
nuclei_min 20 nuclei minimum number of nuclei of a cell type in a donor for a usable pseudobulk sample (criterion E7)
covariates age, sex, genetic ancestry ancestry is strongly unbalanced between groups (Step 3); no post-mortem interval in the file
max_nuclei_per_donor 200 random subsample used only for the Seurat object, so that every donor weighs the same

3 Part A – Study design: who do we compare?

Before looking at any gene, we decide which donors are compared, with criteria fixed in advance, as for a clinical trial. This part only uses the table of the nuclei (donor, diagnoses, age, sex, ancestry, cell type), not the gene expression.

4 Step 1 – The data

What we do and why. The data come from the PsychAD atlas [1], which is shared on CELLxGENE as one file per brain bank. We use the file of the HBCC bank (NIMH Human Brain Collection Core): 1,486,324 nuclei from 300 donors, about 14 GB. The file is downloaded once and kept in 01_DATA/raw/.

Code 
# The data set is downloaded from its CELLxGENE link (h5ad_url, defined in the parameters).
# If the complete file is already in 01_DATA/raw/, it is used as it is.
if (!file.exists(h5ad_file)) {
  dir.create(dirname(h5ad_file), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  options(timeout = 36000)                                    # large file: allow a long download
  download.file(h5ad_url, paste0(h5ad_file, ".part"), mode = "wb")
  file.rename(paste0(h5ad_file, ".part"), h5ad_file)          # renamed only once the download is complete
}
file.size(h5ad_file) / 1e9                                    # size in GB (about 14)
[1] 14.15053

5 Step 2 – Donor selection

What we do and why. We start from the 300 donors of the HBCC brain bank. Using a single bank avoids mixing a difference between banks with a difference between diseases (a “site” confounder). We then apply inclusion and exclusion criteria, as for a clinical trial, starting from the group definitions of Lee et al. [1] and making them stricter on two points.

From nuclei to donors. We keep one row per donor: we want to count people, not nuclei. The age is written as text (“45-year-old stage”, “8-month-old stage”): we convert it to years.

Code 
donors <- donors_from_nuclei(meta)
donors$age <- parse_age(donors$development_stage)

nrow(donors)                                        # expected: 300 donors
[1] 300

One TRUE/FALSE column per diagnosis. The disease column lists all the diagnoses of a donor, separated by || (for example schizophrenia || type 2 diabetes mellitus || tardive dyskinesia). flag_diagnoses() creates one column per diagnosis; whatever is left after removing the known diagnoses is an “other diagnosis” (OCD, epilepsy…). Schizoaffective disorder of bipolar type contains the word “bipolar”, so it is flagged first and removed from the text.

The criteria. Each criterion is one line of select_donors(). A donor is counted once, at the first criterion it fails.

Criterion Rule Why
I2 age at death >= 20 years before 20, the cortex is still maturing [3]: young controls versus adult patients would create a false difference
E1 not both SCZ and BD a donor cannot be in both groups we compare
E2 no schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type in [1] these donors are counted in both SCZ and BD
E4, E5 no other brain disorder (dementia, epilepsy, other psychiatric diagnosis) it would change the cells independently of SCZ or BD (“no secondary diagnosis” rule of [1])
E6 no missing covariate age, sex and ancestry are needed in every model
kept on purpose tardive dyskinesia; controls with diabetes or atherosclerosis part of the real clinical picture; metabolic disorders are tolerated in [1]
Code 
selection <- select_donors(donors, age_min = age_min,
                           keep_td = keep_tardive_dyskinesia,
                           keep_metabolic_controls = keep_metabolic_controls)
donors$group            <- selection$group
donors$exclusion_reason <- selection$reason

sel <- donors[donors$group != "Excluded", ]
sel$group <- factor(sel$group, levels = c("Control", "SCZ", "BD"))
table(sel$group)

age_test

    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  age by group
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 12.288, df = 2, p-value = 0.002146

Figure PP-F01 - Age at death of the selected donors, per group. Violin plot, box plot (median and interquartile range) and individual donors (dots). Only donors aged 20 years or more were kept.

TipHow to read

Each dot is a donor. The box gives the median and the middle half of the ages. If the three violins overlap well, age cannot fully explain a difference between groups; it is still adjusted for in every model.

ImportantInterpretation
  • 224 donors kept out of 300: 121 controls, 49 SCZ and 54 BD.
  • Median ages differ a little between groups (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.002), but the distributions overlap widely: we treat age as a covariate of every model rather than as a reason to exclude more donors.
  • The criterion with the largest effect is the age threshold (58 donors under 20, almost all controls). Thresholds of 17 and 24 years are sensitivity analyses (Step 4).

       title = "Genetic ancestry is strongly unbalanced between the groups",
       subtitle = "Most BD donors are of European ancestry, most SCZ donors of African ancestry") +
  theme_project()
p_PP_F02
save_figure(p_PP_F02, "PP_F02_ancestry_by_group", fig_dir, width = 7, height = 4.5)

ancestry_counts <- table(droplevels(sel$genetic_ancestry), sel$group)
as.data.frame.matrix(ancestry_counts)

Figure PP-F02 - Genetic ancestry of the donors, per group. Share of each genetic ancestry among the donors of each group (counts in the table below the figure).

TipHow to read

Each bar is one group and adds up to 100 %. If the colours had the same shares in the three bars, ancestry would be balanced. Here they clearly do not.

ImportantInterpretation
  • This is the most serious limit of the project. BD donors are mostly of European ancestry (45 of 54) and SCZ donors mostly of African ancestry (32 of 49). Genetic ancestry changes the expression of some genes (eQTL), so comparing SCZ with BD is partly comparing two ancestries (confounding between diagnosis and ancestry).
  • How we handle it: ancestry is a covariate of every model, SCZ vs BD is interpreted with caution, and Q1 adds analyses stratified by ancestry. Controls are better balanced (70 African, 43 European), so each disease can be compared with controls of the same ancestry.
  • Tardive dyskinesia is only found in SCZ (12 (24 %)), as expected for a side effect of antipsychotics.

td_controls <- sum(sel$Tardive_dyskinesia == "Yes" & sel$group == "Control")
TipHow to read

For each yes/no column of the file, agreement with the text of the diagnoses (300 donors). A column with discordant donors cannot be trusted.

ImportantInterpretation
  • The schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and atherosclerosis columns agree 100 % with the diagnoses.
  • The Tardive_dyskinesia column does not (36 discordant donors, including 10 selected controls marked “Yes”), so we use the text of the diagnoses instead.
  • The post-mortem interval (PMI) is not in the file: our covariates are limited to age, sex and ancestry.

7 Step 4 – Sensitivity analyses

What we do and why. We repeat the selection, changing one parameter at a time. These variants are used by the sensitivity analyses of the next questions.

Code 
variants <- list(
  main                       = selection,
  age_17                     = select_donors(donors, 17,      keep_tardive_dyskinesia, keep_metabolic_controls),
  age_24                     = select_donors(donors, 24,      keep_tardive_dyskinesia, keep_metabolic_controls),
  without_tardive_dyskinesia = select_donors(donors, age_min, FALSE,                   keep_metabolic_controls),
  strict_controls            = select_donors(donors, age_min, keep_tardive_dyskinesia, FALSE),
  schizoaff_bipolar_to_SCZ   = select_donors(donors, age_min, keep_tardive_dyskinesia, keep_metabolic_controls, "SCZ"),
  schizoaff_bipolar_to_BD    = select_donors(donors, age_min, keep_tardive_dyskinesia, keep_metabolic_controls, "BD"))

group_levels <- c("Control", "SCZ", "BD", "Excluded")
sensitivity_group_sizes <- t(sapply(variants, function(v) table(factor(v$group, levels = group_levels))))

8 Step 5 – Cell types per donor (input of Q1)

What we do and why. For the composition analysis (Q1), all we need is the number of nuclei of each of the 27 subclasses in each selected donor, using all their nuclei. We also count, for each subclass, how many donors of each group have at least 20 nuclei of it (criterion E7): a subclass that is too rare cannot be analysed in pseudobulk.

9 Part B – Data processing: are the data usable, and in which form?

Now that the donors are chosen, we read their gene expression, check its quality, and put it in the two forms used by the next questions: a Seurat object (one column per nucleus) and a pseudobulk matrix (one column per donor and cell type).

10 Step 6 – Reading the data

What we do and why. The data set is too large to be loaded at once in the memory of a computer (1.5 million nuclei). We therefore read the file one donor at a time: we read the nuclei of a donor, keep what we need, free the memory, then move to the next donor. This works because the nuclei of each donor are stored next to each other in the file (checked for every donor). The reading functions are in scripts/utils_h5ad.R.

Raw counts? The file has no raw/ layer, so the matrix X should hold the raw counts. We read the first million values and check that they are integers.

Code 
test_values <- as.numeric(h5read(h5ad_file, "/X/data", index = list(1:1e6)))
h5closeAll()
all(test_values == round(test_values))     # TRUE = integers = raw counts
[1] TRUE
Code

if (!file.exists(seurat_file)) {
  # 1. Read the drawn nuclei, donor by donor (about 7 minutes)
  counts <- read_chosen_nuclei(h5ad_file, chosen_nuclei, gene_table$name)

  # 2. Metadata of each nucleus, with the information of its donor
  meta_nuclei <- meta[kept_rows, c("donor_id", "class", "subclass", "subtype", "n_counts", "n_genes")]
  rownames(meta_nuclei) <- colnames(counts)
  position <- match(as.character(meta_nuclei$donor_id), sel$donor_id)
  meta_nuclei$group    <- as.character(sel$group[position])
  meta_nuclei$age      <- sel$age[position]
  meta_nuclei$sex      <- sel$sex[position]
  meta_nuclei$ancestry <- as.character(sel$genetic_ancestry[position])

  obj <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = counts, meta.data = meta_nuclei, project = "HBCC_SCZ_BD")
  rm(counts); invisible(gc())

  # 3. The UMAP computed by the authors, to compare it with ours
  umap_authors <- t(h5read(h5ad_file, "/obsm/X_umap")[, kept_rows])
  h5closeAll()
  rownames(umap_authors) <- colnames(obj)
  colnames(umap_authors) <- c("umapAuthors_1", "umapAuthors_2")
  obj[["umap_authors"]] <- CreateDimReducObject(embeddings = umap_authors, key = "umapAuthors_", assay = "RNA")

  saveRDS(obj, seurat_file)        # saved now, and again after the pipeline of Step 8
}

TipWhy we check a ratio and not an exact equality

Our totals are slightly lower than the authors’ (by about 0.5 %) but perfectly correlated with them. A reading error would give random differences and a low correlation: the reading is correct. The small gap probably comes from a longer gene list used by the authors to compute their totals (not tested).

11 Step 7 – Quality control

What we do and why. The authors had already filtered the nuclei [1]. We did not filter again, to stay comparable with the atlas; we checked the distributions on the subsample.

Figure PP-F03 - Quality of the nuclei, per group. Number of RNA molecules per nucleus (nCount_RNA), number of detected genes (nFeature_RNA) and percentage of mitochondrial reads (percent_mt, human pattern ^MT-), on 44,588 nuclei (at most 200 per donor).

TipHow to read

One violin per group and per measure. Similar violins in the three groups mean that the data quality does not differ between controls and patients.

ImportantInterpretation
  • Sharp bounds (never fewer than 983 genes, never more than 1 % mitochondrial reads) show that a filter has already been applied upstream.
  • Mitochondrial reads are almost absent (median 0.08 %) because these are nuclei: mitochondria are in the cytoplasm (single-nucleus RNA-seq). The 5-20 % thresholds used for whole cells do not apply here.
  • SCZ nuclei have about 7 % fewer molecules than controls (medians). This is a nucleus-level description, not a test; depth differences are corrected by the normalisation of each sample.
  • No knee plot can be drawn: the file contains only the nuclei retained by the authors, not all the droplets.

12 Step 8 – Normalisation and visual check of the cell types (PCA, UMAP)

What we do and why. We follow the steps of the course on the subsample. The upstream steps (alignment, filtering, annotation) were done by the authors on the whole atlas [1]: we checked them rather than redoing them.

Step of the pipeline (course video) What it is for What we did
Experimental design (01) decide who is compared with whom 224 donors, one bank, criteria fixed in advance
Count table (02) count the RNA molecules of each gene in each nucleus done by the authors; raw integer counts checked
Quality control (03-04) remove damaged, empty or double nuclei done by the authors; distributions checked (PP-F03)
Normalisation (05) make nuclei comparable despite different amounts of captured RNA NormalizeData(), LogNormalize, scale factor 10,000
Highly variable genes (06) keep the genes that separate cell types FindVariableFeatures(nfeatures = 2000), vst method
Scaling (06) give every gene the same weight in the PCA ScaleData() on the 2,000 variable genes
PCA (08-09) summarise 2,000 genes in a few axes RunPCA(npcs = 30); elbow around 10-15, 30 kept
Clustering (10) group similar cells not redone: 27 subclasses of the authors
UMAP (07, 10) draw a 2D map where similar cells are close RunUMAP(dims = 1:30)
Annotation (11-12) name the cell groups annotation of the authors, checked on our UMAP and with marker genes
Differential expression (13) genes changing between conditions prepared at the donor level (pseudobulk, Step 9)
Integration (bonus) correct batch effects not done: one bank, donors mixed on the UMAP

Why normalise. A nucleus that captured twice as much RNA shows twice as many molecules of every gene without being biologically different. LogNormalize divides each count by the total of the nucleus, multiplies by 10,000 and takes log(1 + x).

Code 
# The pipeline is computed once, then saved with the object
if (!"umap" %in% Reductions(obj)) {
  obj <- NormalizeData(obj)                             # LogNormalize, scale factor 10,000
  obj <- FindVariableFeatures(obj, nfeatures = 2000)    # 2,000 most variable genes (vst)
  obj <- ScaleData(obj)                                 # each variable gene centred and scaled
  obj <- RunPCA(obj, npcs = 30)                         # principal component analysis
  obj <- RunUMAP(obj, dims = 1:30)                      # 2D map from the first 30 components
  saveRDS(obj, seurat_file)
}

Code 
ElbowPlot(obj, ndims = 30) + theme_project() +
  labs(title = "Variance explained by the principal components")

Why 30 principal components. The elbow of the variance plot is around 10 to 15 components. We kept 30 because too few components can erase rare populations (microglia, vascular cells), whereas a few extra components mainly add noise to a map used only for visualisation.

Why we did not re-cluster. The 27 subclasses come from a hierarchical annotation of more than 6 million nuclei [1]. A clustering of a subsample would be less reliable and not comparable with the atlas.

Code

Figure PP-F04 - UMAP of 44,588 nuclei coloured by cell subclass. UMAP computed on the first 30 principal components of the 2,000 most variable genes; subclasses as annotated by the authors [1].

TipHow to read

Each dot is a nucleus; nuclei with similar gene expression are close. Distances between islands are not meaningful, only which nuclei group together.

ImportantInterpretation
  • The 27 subclasses form separate islands, as in the authors’ UMAP: our pipeline recovers their annotation, which validates the reading of the data.
  • Excitatory neurons (EN), inhibitory neurons (IN), oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, OPC, microglia and vascular cells each form their own islands.

Do the cell types express their known marker genes? The UMAP shows that the 27 subclasses form separate islands. We also check that each subclass expresses its marker genes, as in the annotation step of a single-cell analysis. We use two sources linked to our data set:

  • the marker genes chosen by the authors of the atlas [1]: Figure 2d of [1] for the neuronal subclasses (two per subclass), and, for the other cell types, the subclass-level markers of the gene panel that the authors designed for their spatial transcriptomics experiment (Supplementary Table 10 of [1]; this panel had room for about 100 genes, so it keeps one to three of the most specific genes per subclass);
  • the marker genes of the cell taxonomy that the authors used to name the cell types, Ma et al. 2022 [5].

No marker gene is given for adaptive immune cells in these sources: they are not shown.

TipHow to read

Each row is a gene, each column a subclass. The size of a dot is the percentage of nuclei of the subclass that express the gene; its colour is the mean expression. A good marker gives a large dark dot in its own subclass and small pale dots elsewhere: if the annotation is right, the dark dots form a diagonal.

The same check in numbers. For each marker gene, we look for the subclass where its mean expression is the highest, and compare it with the subclass it is supposed to mark.

Code 
shown <- c(neuron_subclasses, other_subclasses)
in_shown <- obj$subclass %in% shown
expression <- LayerData(obj, layer = "data")[unique(marker_table$gene), in_shown]
subclass_of_nuclei <- factor(obj$subclass[in_shown], levels = shown)
membership <- fac2sparse(subclass_of_nuclei)                       # subclasses x nuclei, 1 = belongs
mean_expression <- as.matrix(expression %*% t(membership)) / rep(rowSums(membership), each = nrow(expression))
highest <- setNames(colnames(mean_expression)[apply(mean_expression, 1, which.max)], rownames(mean_expression))

marker_table$highest_in <- highest[marker_table$gene]
# A gene that marks several subclasses (e.g. RORB) is correct if it is highest in one of them
expected_sets <- tapply(marker_table$expected, paste(marker_table$gene, marker_table$source), unique)
marker_table$match <- mapply(function(g, s, h) h %in% expected_sets[[paste(g, s)]],
                             marker_table$gene, marker_table$source, marker_table$highest_in)

n_match   <- sum(marker_table$match)
n_markers <- nrow(marker_table)
aggregate(match ~ source, data = marker_table, FUN = function(x) paste0(sum(x), " / ", length(x)))

67 of 77 marker genes are highest in their expected subclass. The table above lists the exceptions.

ImportantInterpretation
  • 67 of 77 marker genes are highest in their expected subclass, including all 18 markers of the non-neuronal subclasses chosen by the authors and 31 of the 34 neuronal markers of their Figure 2d: our data reproduce the diagonal of Figure 2d of [1], which confirms both our reading of the file and the annotation of the authors.
  • The three exceptions from Figure 2d are near misses. THEMIS is highest in EN_L6_IT_2 rather than EN_L6_IT_1, but it marks both L6 IT subclasses, as in Figure 2d. TRPC3 and MAFB are highest in a non-neuronal subclass (pericytes, perivascular macrophages), but among neurons they mark their own subclass (Figure PP-F05).
  • The markers of the primate taxonomy [5] agree less well (18 of 25), mostly because some of them mark broader groups than our subclasses: LHX6 marks all the interneurons of one developmental origin (SST, PVALB, LAMP5_LHX6), ADARB2 and RELN those of the other origin (VIP, ADARB2, LAMP5_RELN), and FEZF2 all deep-layer neurons. SYT6 and CCN2 are highest in a non-neuronal subclass (microglia, VLMC), but among neurons they mark EN_L6_CT and EN_L6B (Figure PP-F05). PCDH8 does not mark EN_L2_3_IT in our data.

Figure PP-F07 - UMAP of 44,588 nuclei coloured by diagnosis. Same UMAP as Figure PP-F04.

TipHow to read

If one diagnosis formed its own island, the disease would create a new cell state. Mixed colours mean that the same cell types are found in the three groups.

ImportantInterpretation
  • Controls, SCZ and BD are mixed in every island: the diseases do not create new cell types.
  • A few small areas look dominated by one colour, for example the lower part of the astrocyte island (mostly BD). We checked it by selecting this area by eye on the UMAP (exploratory check, not reproduced by the code): it holds 386 nuclei, 72 % of them from BD donors, versus 25 % BD among all astrocytes; but 3 BD donors bring 35 % of its nuclei. The area therefore mostly reflects a few people, not the disease. A similar area of the OPC (36 % BD versus 28 %) has no dominant donor. A coloured area of a UMAP is not a result: only a donor-level test can conclude (Q1, Q2).

13 Step 9 – Pseudobulk: one sample per donor and cell type (input of Q2 and Q5)

What we do and why. For each donor, we sort its nuclei by cell type and add up their counts, gene by gene. For example, all the microglia of donor 1 become one “sample”, all its astrocytes another one. We obtain one sample per donor and cell type, as if the cells of each type had been sorted and sequenced together (pseudobulk). Each donor then counts once in the tests, which avoids treating 5,000 nuclei of the same brain as 5,000 people [2]. We use all the nuclei here, not the 200-nuclei subsample. This matrix is the input of Q2 and Q5.

The 27 cell types are kept for every donor, even when a donor has none of a type (empty sample): Q2 removes the samples with too few nuclei (E7 threshold).

Code 
if (!file.exists(pseudobulk_file)) {
  pb <- build_pseudobulk(h5ad_file, meta, sel, gene_table$name)     # about 10 minutes
  saveRDS(pb, pseudobulk_file)
  write.csv(pb$description, file.path(proc_dir, "pseudobulk_column_description.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
}

15 Limits

  • Ancestry confounded with diagnosis (severity 5/5): adjusted for and stratified, but it cannot be removed.
  • QC and doublet detection not redone (3/5): we rely on the filtering of the authors [1].
  • No post-mortem interval and no information on treatments (3/5): covariates limited to age, sex and ancestry.
  • Subsample of 200 nuclei per donor (2/5): used only for the Seurat object; every statistical analysis uses all nuclei.
  • Donors with few nuclei (2/5): 12 donors with fewer than 1,000 nuclei (minimum 61).
